title: Freelancing Basics
description: Rates, invoices, late payers and quarterly taxes.
wolfLine: When you hunt alone, you carry your own kill. Price accordingly.

freelancer.definition: Someone who sells their skills to clients, project by project, instead of working for one employer.
freelancer.example: A designer making logos for several small businesses.

invoice.definition: The bill you send a client: what you did, what it costs, and when it’s due.

payment-terms.definition: The deadline for a client to pay you. “Net 30” means within 30 days of the invoice date.

business-expense.definition: A cost of running your work, like software, equipment or a website. Many lower the profit you’re taxed on.

estimated-taxes.definition: Tax payments self-employed people make four times a year, since nothing is taken out of their pay.
estimated-taxes.example: Paying the IRS on April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.

lessons.title: Working for Yourself
lessons.summary: Freedom, clients, and everything an employer used to handle.

steps.context: A [[freelancer]] sells their skills to clients, project by project, instead of working for one employer.
steps.prompt: Which is freelancing?
choices: Designing logos for several small businesses
steps.explain: Many clients, one project at a time.

steps.prompt: What does a freelancer handle that an employer usually would?
choices: Finding clients, taxes, health insurance and retirement
steps.explain: You’re the boss, and also the payroll department.

steps.prompt: Freelancers can choose which clients and projects to take.
steps.explain: One of the best parts.

steps.prompt: What’s a smart way to start?
choices: Alongside a job, with a few clients first
Quit with no clients and no savings
steps.explain: Prove it before you leap.

steps.prompt: You need $3,000 a month to live and have $9,000 saved. How many months can savings carry you while you build clients?
Freelancers are paid by ___, not by an employer’s payroll.
steps.explain: Every client is a little paycheck.

lessons.title: Setting Your Rate
lessons.summary: Work backwards from what you need.

steps.title: Work backwards
steps.body:
Start from what you want to earn in a year, add your business costs, then divide by the hours you can actually bill.

Not every hour is billable. Finding clients, emails and admin are unpaid.

steps.prompt: You want $50,000 a year for yourself, plus $5,000 of business costs. How much must you bring in?
You can bill about 1,100 hours a year. What hourly rate do you need?
Why only 1,100 billable hours, when a full-time year is about 2,080?
choices: Much of your time goes to finding clients and admin
steps.explain: Plan for roughly half your hours being unpaid.

steps.prompt: Raise your rate from $50 to $60 an hour. Over 1,100 hours, how much more do you earn?
Charging too little at the start makes it harder to raise prices later.
steps.explain: Clients anchor on your first price.

lessons.title: Hourly or Per Project?
lessons.summary: Two ways to price the same job.

steps.context: Hourly means you’re paid for time. Per project means one fixed price for the whole job.
steps.prompt: You quote $2,400 for a website project. It takes you 30 hours. What did you earn per hour?
It takes 48 hours instead. Per hour now?
Which pricing rewards you for getting faster?
steps.explain: Finish sooner, earn more per hour.

steps.prompt: Which protects you when a client keeps adding changes?
choices: Hourly, or a project price with a set number of revisions
steps.explain: Define what’s included.

steps.prompt: Writing down exactly what’s included protects both you and the client.
steps.explain: No surprises on either side.

steps.prompt: The client asks for “just one more small thing” for the fifth time. Your move?
choices: Point to the agreement and quote the extra work
steps.explain: Friendly, firm, and in writing.

lessons.title: Send an Invoice
lessons.summary: The bill that gets you paid.

steps.context: An [[invoice]] is the bill you send a client: what you did, what it costs, and when it’s due.

doc.title: Invoice #0042
doc.subtitle: From: Rosa Diaz Design · To: Sunny Side Bakery
doc.note: Payment terms: net 30. Late payments add 1.5% a month.

steps.prompt: When is this invoice due?
steps.explain: The due date, top right.

doc.title: Invoice #0042
doc.subtitle: From: Rosa Diaz Design · To: Sunny Side Bakery
doc.note: Payment terms: net 30. Late payments add 1.5% a month.

steps.prompt: What’s the total due?

steps.context: [[Payment terms]] say when you must be paid. “Net 30” means within 30 days of the invoice date.

doc.title: Invoice #0042
doc.subtitle: From: Rosa Diaz Design · To: Sunny Side Bakery
doc.note: Payment terms: net 30. Late payments add 1.5% a month.

steps.prompt: What does “net 30” mean here?
steps.explain: Mar 3 plus 30 days is Apr 2.

doc.title: Invoice #0042
doc.subtitle: From: Rosa Diaz Design · To: Sunny Side Bakery
doc.note: Payment terms: net 30. Late payments add 1.5% a month.

steps.prompt: If it’s paid a month late, what’s the 1.5% late fee on $1,290?
Number every invoice and keep a copy.
steps.explain: You’ll need them for taxes and for chasing late payers.

steps.prompt: What gets an invoice paid faster?
choices: A clear due date and easy ways to pay
steps.explain: Make paying you effortless.

steps.prompt: What’s the best protection on a big project?
steps.explain: Half before you start, half when you finish.

steps.prompt: What’s a 50% deposit on a $2,400 project?
A client is late. Put your steps in order.
items: Follow up with the invoice and late fee
Pause new work until they pay
steps.explain: Polite, then firmer, then stop working for free.

steps.prompt: Clients paying 30 to 60 days after the work means you need savings to cover the gap.
steps.explain: Your rent doesn’t wait for net 30.

steps.prompt: You invoice $4,000 on Mar 31, net 30. When should you expect the money?
steps.explain: 30 days after the invoice.

steps.prompt: A client never pays $800, even after reminders. Last resort?
choices: Small claims court, often without a lawyer
steps.explain: Small claims is built for exactly this.

lessons.title: Business Expenses
lessons.summary: What counts, and why receipts matter.

steps.context: A [[business expense]] is a cost of running your work: software, equipment, a website. Many of them lower the profit you’re taxed on.
steps.prompt: Which is a business expense for a freelance designer?
steps.explain: Used for the work.

steps.prompt: Business or personal?
Income $40,000, business expenses $6,000. What’s the profit?
Setting aside about 25% of profit for taxes, how much?
Keeping receipts for business expenses matters at tax time.
steps.explain: No receipt, no proof.

steps.prompt: What’s the easiest way to keep track?
choices: A separate account and card just for business
steps.explain: One account, one clean record.

lessons.title: Quarterly Taxes
lessons.summary: Four deadlines a year, and how to be ready.

steps.context: Self-employed people usually pay [[estimated taxes]] four times a year, since nothing is taken out of their pay.
steps.prompt: How often are estimated taxes usually paid?
steps.explain: Quarterly.

steps.prompt: Put the estimated tax due dates in order, starting in spring.
steps.explain: Not quite every three months, so put them in your calendar.

steps.prompt: You set aside 25% of $2,800 profit each month. How much over a quarter (3 months)?
Missing estimated tax payments can mean penalties.
steps.explain: Late payments add interest and penalties.

steps.prompt: Where should tax money wait until it’s due?
steps.explain: Earning a little interest, out of reach.

steps.prompt: Not sure how much to pay?
choices: Ask a tax pro or follow the IRS guide. It’s worth it the first year
steps.explain: The Taxes section of this course goes deeper too.

lessons.title: Rosa’s First Freelance Year
lessons.summary: More money billed. Is it more money earned?

story.title: Year one on her own
story.body:
Rosa left her job in January with **$12,000** saved. By December she had billed clients **$58,000**.

But one client, Bluefin, still owes her **$3,500**. Her business expenses (software, a new laptop, her website) came to **$7,000**. She set aside **25%** of her profit for taxes.

Her old job paid **$45,000**, with health insurance and a 401(k) match.

steps.prompt: What did Rosa actually collect this year?
What’s her profit, using what she collected minus $7,000 of expenses?
25% of profit for taxes?
What’s left for Rosa to live on?
Her old job paid $45,000 with health insurance and a match. Is freelancing paying more yet?
choices: Not yet: she now covers insurance and retirement herself
steps.explain: Billing more isn’t the same as keeping more.

steps.prompt: What would help most next year?
choices: Deposits upfront and a higher rate
steps.explain: Get paid sooner, and get paid more.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Freelancing
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: 3 hours at $75 an hour, plus $50 of stock images, on one invoice. Total?
What does “net 30” mean?
choices: Pay within 30 days of the invoice date
steps.explain: 30 days to pay.

steps.prompt: Freelancers have taxes taken out of their pay automatically.
steps.explain: They pay estimated taxes themselves.

steps.prompt: $3,000 of profit this month. Set aside 25% for taxes. How much?
